title: Gentle pitch and counting
purpose: Explore a slightly higher, comfortable pitch while keeping resonance forward.
instructions: Warm up with a few gentle pitch glides.
Breathe in through your nose and hum gently at your usual speaking pitch a few times. Keep the vibration in your face, lips and nose.
Hum slightly higher than your usual speaking pitch. Don't go too high or too fast. Aim for a smooth sound.
Keeping that slightly higher hum, count from one to five, then breathe normally. Repeat a few times.
When this feels comfortable, try counting to twenty.

primary_cue.text: Only slightly higher than usual, with the vibration still in your face.

cues.text: Only slightly higher than usual, with the vibration still in your face.
Go back to the forward hum at your usual pitch until the vibration is in your face again, then go up only a little.

practice_task.prompt_text: Hum slightly higher than usual, then count: one, two, three, four, five.

check_questions.text: Could you keep the slightly higher pitch and the forward vibration while counting?
Did it sound like you, or cartoon-like?

dose_guidance.text: The source gives no repetition count beyond “a few times”. It says this takes time and concentration, and to be patient with yourself.

expected_observations: The source says a higher pitch can sound cartoon-like when resonance stays low, which is why resonance comes first.
common_misunderstandings: Pitch is one part of the voice, not the whole goal. A measured number cannot show how feminine a voice is.
Higher is not automatically better. Choose a comfortable level that sounds like you.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
adaptations: Stay at counting to five for as long as you need.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
The source also describes a voice-box (larynx) instruction. Lilt does not present it as a cue; read the source or ask a voice clinician.
Lilt shows pitch measurements for description only. They are not validated for coaching and never set a target for you.
